speaker: David Baker
title: Nobel Laureate David Baker on Using AI for Science to Solve Humanity's Biggest Problems
question: In AI for science, what determines whether a generalist machine learning team or a deep domain-specialist lab has the structural advantage on a scientific problem?
guest: It depends on what the problem is. Even if we just look in the realm of proteins, there's protein structure prediction and protein design. In structure prediction, the very large number of protein structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank actually contained enough information to solve the problem. It's a very well-posed ML problem because you have a large amount of data, and you can just compare your predicted structure to the actual structure to see how well you're doing. Protein design, even though it's the inverse problem, is much more open-ended because you want to design new proteins that do new and interesting things—but what should those things be? And it's not purely a computational problem. Say you want to design a protein to cure cancer: you do your design calculation and have an amino acid sequence, but there's no way of knowing whether that sequence cures cancer without making and testing it. When we started developing AI methods for protein design, we already knew what the important problems were and how to make and experimentally test proteins. So whether the generalist or the domain specialist wins really depends on the nature of the problem.

points.core: Generalist AI teams dominate well-posed problems with abundant existing ground-truth datasets.
points.note: Accept: pure ML groups win when large curated training datasets already define a clear input-output mapping (e.g. PDB for structure prediction). Do not credit: generic claims that AI needs data without tying data completeness to generalist advantage.

points.core: Generalist models thrive when predictions can be verified computationally against known ground truth.
points.note: Accept: clear objective benchmarks or automated in-silico scoring loops allow AI-first teams to iterate rapidly without wet labs. Do not credit: vague mentions of good metrics without contrasting computational verification against physical testing.

points.core: Open-ended scientific design problems require deep domain judgment to choose meaningful targets.
points.note: Accept: generative or inverse-design tasks lack a fixed target, so domain experts are needed to define which real-world functions or problems matter. Do not credit: platitudes that domain knowledge is helpful.

points.core: Domain labs win when validating outputs requires physical synthesis inside wet-lab experiments.
points.note: Accept: when computational scores cannot prove real-world efficacy (e.g. whether a designed protein treats disease), experimental lab infrastructure and assay expertise become decisive. Do not credit: generic statements that experiments are expensive.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The advantage mostly turns on where the bottleneck sits: in modeling and compute, or in data, problem formulation and validation.

Generalist ML teams tend to win when the problem is already "benchmark-shaped": a large, clean, standardized public dataset exists, the objective is crisply defined, and success can be scored computationally. Protein structure prediction is the canonical case. The PDB and CASP gave decades of curated data and a clear metric, so architecture skill, engineering and scale became the scarce inputs. Weather forecasting on ERA5 reanalysis followed the same pattern.

Domain-specialist labs tend to win when data is scarce, noisy, proprietary or has to be generated by experiment. They also win when knowing which question matters requires tacit knowledge, and when validation needs wet-lab or physical feedback loops rather than a held-out test set. There, the limiting factors are owning the data-generating instrument, understanding the artifacts and confounders, and judging whether a prediction is scientifically meaningful.

Secondary factors include how much prior physical structure must be built into the model and whether foundation models transfer to it. This is why the strongest efforts increasingly combine both, pairing ML scale with in-house experimental capacity.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
The structural advantage hinges primarily on how cleanly a scientific problem can be decoupled from physical experimentation into a static, well-posed computational benchmark. Generalist machine learning teams excel when a domain already possesses large, standardized datasets—or fast, high-fidelity simulators—paired with an unambiguous evaluation metric, as seen in protein structure prediction or medium-range weather forecasting. Once a problem is cleanly abstracted into inputs, outputs, and a reliable loss function, progress is bottlenecked by compute scale, engineering velocity, and general-purpose architectural optimization rather than specialized theory.

Conversely, deep domain-specialist labs hold the advantage when the core bottleneck lies in problem formulation, proprietary data generation, or tight, iterative experimental loops. Where observations are scarce, heterogeneous, and confounded by instrument-specific artifacts, tacit knowledge of measurement error, causal mechanisms, and exact physical symmetries becomes decisive. Until a domain’s data acquisition and validation can be standardized into an offline digital benchmark, direct control over physical instruments, wet-lab verification, and mechanistic priors outweighs raw scaling expertise.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The deciding factor is where the problem's main bottleneck sits: in learning from data that already exists, or in defining the problem, producing the data and checking the results.

A generalist ML team has the edge when the problem is already well posed. That usually means a large, curated public dataset, a clear objective metric or benchmark, and a fairly clean input-to-output mapping. In that setting, scale, engineering skill, compute and transferable architectures decide the outcome. AlphaFold is the standard example: the Protein Data Bank and the CASP competition had already turned a hard biology problem into a learning problem, so DeepMind's ML strength could dominate.

A domain-specialist lab has the edge when the hard part comes before or after the model. That covers knowing which question matters and how to represent it, data that is scarce or has to be generated through experiments, tacit knowledge about noise and artifacts, and success that can only be confirmed through lab work, field work or expert judgment. Here the advantage comes from owning the experimental loop and the hard-won judgment, both of which are slow to acquire.

The advantage also shifts over time. Once specialists build good datasets and benchmarks, a problem becomes legible to generalists. And when an ML team builds or partners for its own data generation and lab validation, it effectively becomes a specialist lab.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
The structural advantage depends primarily on where the bottleneck sits: modeling at scale versus experimental generation and physical framing. Generalist machine learning teams hold the advantage when a field already has large, standardized, high-signal datasets—or fast, faithful simulators—paired with unambiguous evaluation metrics. In settings like protein structure prediction or medium-range weather forecasting, once the problem is cleanly abstracted, progress is driven by scaling compute, architectural breakthroughs, and representation learning rather than bespoke domain heuristics.

Deep domain-specialist labs hold the advantage when data are scarce, noisy, or expensive to produce, and when the core challenge is closing the loop with physical reality. In wet-lab biology, novel materials synthesis, or complex instrumentation, knowing which experiments to run, recognizing subtle artifacts, encoding physical constraints, and validating predictions in the real world matter more than raw modeling sophistication. Ultimately, generalists win when scientific discovery can be compressed into a well-posed prediction problem at scale, while specialists win when formulating the question, generating trustworthy data, and navigating physical validation remain the rate-limiting steps.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The structural advantage goes to the team better positioned to resolve the problem’s main bottleneck. Generalist machine learning teams have the edge when the scientific objective is well specified, data are accessible, and models can be tested quickly against reliable benchmarks or simulators. Under those conditions, advances in architecture, training, and compute can transfer across fields.

Domain-specialist labs have the edge when progress depends on knowing which questions matter, generating measurements that others cannot easily obtain, spotting artifacts, or designing experiments that distinguish competing explanations. Their advantage is strongest when feedback is slow or expensive and a model can score well on a benchmark while missing the scientific point.

The balance can shift within a single project. A generalist team may build the strongest predictor, while a specialist lab is better positioned to turn its predictions into a validated discovery.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
The structural advantage depends on where the bottleneck lies and who can tell whether a result is genuinely better. A generalist machine learning team has the edge when the scientific goal can be expressed as a reliable prediction or optimization target, relevant data are abundant, and candidate solutions can be tested cheaply. Under those conditions, better models, compute, and engineering can translate directly into scientific progress.

A domain-specialist lab has the edge when progress depends on choosing the right question, making a difficult measurement, or designing an experiment that distinguishes between plausible explanations. If a model can generate a thousand candidates overnight but only five can be tested this year, the ability to choose and interpret those five matters more than the ability to generate another thousand.

That advantage can shift. A specialist lab that develops a fast, reliable assay can turn an experiment-limited problem into one where machine learning expertise becomes decisive.
